title: PRAXIS Mission
tags: Achievements of Indians in Science & Technology
content:
NASA
has selected
PRAXIS (Planetary Rings Autonomous EXploration with In-situ Sampling)
for
Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) 2026 Phase I funding
. The mission concept proposes a
first-of-its-kind approach
to directly sample particles from planetary ring systems.

Humanity has
never directly touched or collected particles from a planetary ring
. Such samples could transform our understanding of the rings around
Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
, and smaller objects such as Chariklo and Chiron.
Nature of Saturn’s Rings:
Saturn’s rings
are
composed mainly of water ice
and contain particles ranging from microscopic grains to house-sized boulders. These particles are constantly moving, colliding, combining, and breaking apart.
Background:
Although
NASA’s Cassini mission
made groundbreaking discoveries about Saturn, major questions remain about how planetary rings form, evolve, move, and eventually disappear.
About:
PRAXIS would provide the
first close-up observations of millimetre- to centimetre-sized particles,
a capability Cassini lacked.
Objective:
The mission aims to measure the
size, porosity, structure, and chemical composition of ring particles.
These measurements could explain ring features such as density waves, gaps, propellers, and self-gravity wakes.
AI-Powered Robotic System :
PRAXIS would use an
AI-driven, bio-inspired robotic explorer
capable of autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, target selection, precision sampling, and real-time scientific analysis.
Sampling Method:
Instead of flying directly through the
hazardous ring environment,
the spacecraft would graze the ring plane, identify a suitable particle, and conduct a touch-and-go sampling operation using a long, soft, deployable boom.
Exploration of Multiple Regions:
After retrieving and analysing a sample, the
spacecraft would move to another section or gap in the rings.
Repeating this process would allow scientists to
compare particles from several different ring environments.
Future Potential:
During
NIAC Phase I, the team will test PRAXIS through simulations and detailed system design
. Selection for Phase II would support the construction of physical prototypes, laboratory testing, feasibility demonstrations, and further development of operational strategies.

title: Gen Z Protests: Redefining Democratic Participation in India
tags: Effects of Globalization on Indian Society
content:
For Prelims:
Anna Hazare Movement
,
Assam Accord
,
Gig economy
,
Orange Economy
For Mains:
Generation Z and the changing nature of democratic participation in India., Challenge of India's demographic dividend, Evolution of youth movements in post-Independence India.

Why in News?

A wave of
Generation Z-led demonstrations
, spearheaded by the satirical yet influential
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)
, has emerged over alleged irregularities in the
National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET)
,
rising graduate unemployment, and the growing financial burden of education.

Drawing global comparisons with Gen Z-led political movements in Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, and Peru
, the protests have brought
youth aspirations, civic participation, and demands for greater accountability and systemic reforms
to the forefront of public discourse.

Summary
Generation Z-led protests have emerged as a powerful force in India and globally, highlighting concerns over examination integrity, youth unemployment, rising education costs, and democratic participation while reshaping the nature of political mobilisation.
Addressing youth disillusionment requires comprehensive reforms in education, employment, examination governance, mental health, and youth participation to transform India's demographic dividend into a sustainable youth dividend.

How are Gen Z Protests Reshaping Global Politics?

Generation Z (Gen Z):
Also known as "Zoomers", is the demographic cohort that succeeds the
Millennials and precedes Generation Alpha
.
It broadly comprises individuals born between the mid-1990s and early 2010s, and is characterised by digital nativity, social media engagement, and heightened civic and political awareness.
Role in Politics: Generation Z
has emerged as a significant political force, mobilising through
social media
against
corruption, unemployment, inequality, and governance failures
.
Unlike traditional political movements, these protests are
decentralised, digitally coordinated, and youth-driven
.
Several countries have witnessed
policy reversals, government changes, and political reforms
due to sustained youth mobilisation.
Global Examples:

Country
Trigger
Outcome
Bangladesh
Student-led job quota protests
Sheikh Hasina's government was ousted
;
Muhammad Yunus
became interim leader before fresh elections.
Nepal
Anti-corruption protests
The government changed
; youth-backed leadership emerged.
Indonesia
Lawmakers' privileges amid economic hardship
The government rolled back several controversial measures.
Peru
Crime and political instability
Political instability intensified with successive leadership changes.
India
NEET paper leak and examination reforms
The government accepted several demands, including the
Education Minister's resignation
.

How have Youth Movements Evolved in India?

Ideological Politics (1950s–1960s):
Youth movements were largely
campus-centric
and shaped by
Left- and Right-wing student organisations
such as
SFI (Students' Federation of India), and ABVP (Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad).
Primary concerns included
language, education, and ideological mobilisation
.
Key Developments:
Anti-Hindi Agitation (1965)
in Tamil Nadu.
Naxalbari Movement (1967)
, influenced by
Marxist-Leninist ideology
, with active student participation.
Anti-Establishment and Democratic Mobilisation (1970s
): Student movements expanded beyond campuses to challenge
corruption, inflation, and authoritarian governance
.
Key Developments:
Nav Nirman Andolan (1974)
in Gujarat.
Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) Movement (1974–75)
against corruption and misuse of power.
Student mobilisation contributed to the political developments preceding the
Emergency (1975–77)
.
Identity, Regionalism, and Social Justice (1980s–1990s):
Youth movements increasingly revolved around
regional identity, migration, and affirmative action
.
Key Developments:
Assam Agitation (1979–85)
led by the
All Assam Students' Union (AASU)
, culminating in the
Assam Accord (1985)
.
Anti-Mandal Commission Protests (1990)
over reservation in public employment and education.
Rights-Based Activism (2000s–2010s):
The expansion of the
internet and social media
shifted youth activism towards
transparency, accountability, and civil rights
.
Key Developments:
Anna Hazare Movement (2011)
,
popularly known as the
India Against Corruption (IAC) Movement
, which mobilised millions of young people demanding the
Jan Lokpal Bill
to combat corruption.
Nirbhaya Protests (2012)
,
which led to significant reforms in
criminal laws related to women's safety
and highlighted the role of youth in demanding gender justice.
Gen Z and Issue-Based Activism (2020s–Present):
Contemporary youth movements are
digitally driven, decentralised, and centred on education, employment, governance, and social justice
.
Key Developments:
Anti-CAA/NRC campus protests (2019–20)
.
Agnipath protests (2022)
.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement (2026)
over alleged
NEET paper leaks
, unemployment, and the rising cost of education.

Major Shifts in Youth Movements

From Charismatic Leaders to Decentralised Networks:
Movements have evolved from being led by personalities such as
Jayaprakash Narayan
and
Anna Hazare
to
leaderless, digitally coordinated campaigns
.
From Ideology to Issue-Based Activism:
The focus has shifted from ideological politics to
practical concerns
such as
education reforms, examination integrity, unemployment, climate action, and gig economy rights
.
From Party-Linked to Independent Mobilisation:
Many recent movements operate
outside traditional political parties
, relying on
digital satire, memes, and online campaigns
to mobilise support.
From Physical to Hybrid Protest Models:
While earlier mobilisation depended on prolonged street campaigns, modern movements combine
social media activism with on-ground demonstrations
, enabling rapid and widespread mobilisation.
From Campus Issues to National Policy Debates:
Youth movements today increasingly influence discussions on
education policy, employment, governance, democratic accountability, and institutional reforms
, making them significant actors in public policymaking.

What are the Underlying Causes of Youth Disillusionment in India?

Macroeconomic Asymmetries: The "Educated Unemployed"

Jobless Growth and Skill Mismatch:
The Indian economy is expanding, but it is failing to create formal, remunerative jobs at a pace necessary to absorb the youth bulge.
The
ILO India Employment Report 2024
highlighted a grim reality: youth account for
83% of India’s unemployed workforce
.
More alarmingly, the
jobless rate for graduates stands at a staggering 29.1%
, which is nearly nine times higher than the rate for those without schooling (3.4%).
The rapid adoption of
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
and automation is further disrupting entry-level and routine jobs, with the
World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025
projecting that
92 million jobs could be displaced globally by 2030
, even as new AI-driven roles emerge, underscoring the urgency of large-scale reskilling and upskilling.
Informalization of the Formal Sector:
The limited jobs being generated are heavily concentrated in the precarious
"gig economy."
This deprives the youth of social security, predictable career progression, and economic dignity, perpetuating chronic financial anxiety.
Educational Inflation:
The aggressive privatization of higher education has led to a mass proliferation of degrees without a
concurrent rise in market-relevant skills.
This has severely devalued academic qualifications, leading to a scenario where a university degree no longer guarantees economic security.

Institutional Decay and Compromised Meritocracy

The Shattered Social Contract:
For the vast middle and lower-middle classes,
competitive examinations
(like NEET, UPSC, and state-level commissions) represent the only
legitimate vehicle for upward
social mobility.
The persistent crisis of paper leaks, proxy candidates, and recruitment delays shatters the
foundational belief in a meritocratic state.
State Apathy and Regulatory Deficit:
The failure of regulatory oversight over testing infrastructure, combined with the
unchecked hyper-commercialization of the "coaching hub" industry,
has transformed education into an
exclusionary, profit-driven enterprise
rather than an
equalizing public good.

Sociological and Psychological Dimensions

Institutional Anomie & Relative Deprivation:
Drawing from sociologist Émile Durkheim’s framework, Indian youth are experiencing severe
anomie
(a structural breakdown resulting from the disconnect between the culturally celebrated goals of financial success and the institutional means available to achieve them).
Furthermore, constant exposure to global lifestyles via digital media exacerbates feelings of
relative deprivation
.
The Silent Epidemic of Student Suicides:
The intersection of financial debt (education loans) and exam failure is exacting a catastrophic psychological toll.
According to the
NCRB’s
Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India (ADSI) 2024 report
, young and middle-aged adults (18-45) account for
65.6%
of all suicides.
Alarmingly, the proportion of student suicides has climbed to
8.5% of total cases in 2024
, with tragic clusters forming in hyper-competitive coaching capitals like Kota, Chennai,and Thrissur.
Brain Drain:
Persistent systemic failures, such as
paper leaks, examination cancellations, and recruitment delays
, are accelerating
brain drain
,
as not only top-tier talent but also middle-class youth increasingly seek stable education and employment opportunities abroad, draining India of human and financial capital.

Political Economy and Democratic Alienation

Failure of Interest Aggregation:
Traditional political structures heavily prioritize
identity politics (caste, religion, regionalism) and
welfare populism
aimed at older or rural voter bases.
The
material anxieties of Gen Z
(housing, inflation, and white-collar job creation) remain largely unaddressed in mainstream political mandates.
Shrinking Spaces for Dissent:
When institutional channels fail, youth mobilize on the streets.
However, the state’s default response has increasingly shifted toward
"regime policing"
- deploying prohibitory orders (e.g.,
Section 163 of the BNSS
),
internet shutdowns,
and digital surveillance rather than facilitating constructive policy dialogue. This criminalization of
dissent deepens democratic alienation.

Click here to Read:
Public Examinations Amendment Bill, 2026 and Nandan Nilekani-Led Task Force on Exam Reforms

What Measures are Needed to Address Youth Discontent and Strengthen Democratic Participation?

Move from "Demographic Dividend" to "Youth Dividend":
Adopt a
'Youth in All Policies (YiAP)'
framework, similar to
Finland's Youth Policy
, requiring every major policy on education, employment, climate, and technology to assess its impact on young people.
Expand New-Age Employment Ecosystems:
Move beyond conventional jobs by promoting the
Orange Economy (creative industries)
,
Creator Economy
,
Sports Economy
,
Care Economy
,
Space Economy
, and
Green Economy
through dedicated financing, startup incubation, and intellectual property support.
Institutionalise Youth Participation in Governance:
Establish a
National Youth Council
on the lines of
Singapore's National Youth Council
and strengthen
Youth Parliaments
to provide structured participation in policymaking rather than limiting youth engagement to protests.
Restore Trust in Meritocracy:
Strengthen the
Fast-Track Special Courts (FTSCs)
under the
Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024
with adequate infrastructure, judicial manpower, and technological support to ensure the timely disposal of paper leak cases and uphold the integrity of public examinations.
Simultaneously, undertake comprehensive reforms of the
National Testing Agency (NTA)
by making it an autonomous
body
and adopting
blockchain-based credential verification, zero-trust examination architecture, AI-enabled surveillance, and end-to-end encrypted digital testing infrastructure
to restore public confidence in merit-based examinations.
Reimagine Education for the Fourth Industrial Revolution:
Fully implement
National Education Policy, 2020
by integrating
AI, entrepreneurship, climate literacy, digital public infrastructure, financial literacy, and design thinking
into higher education while making apprenticeships an integral part of every degree programme.
Build a National Youth Well-being Mission:
Drawing lessons from
Australia's Headspace
and the
United Kingdom's student mental health framework
, institutionalise counselling, career guidance, and suicide prevention services across schools, universities, and coaching institutions.
Create Multiple Pathways to Success:
Reduce dependence on single high-stakes examinations by expanding
PARAKH
, introducing
multiple testing windows
, recognising
micro-credentials
, and encouraging
skill-based hiring
, similar to approaches adopted in countries such as
Germany
and
Singapore
.
Leverage Digital Democracy:
Enhance participatory governance
by strengthening
MyGov
into a secure, interactive digital consultation platform where young citizens can contribute to
draft policies, budgets, and legislation
, drawing inspiration from
Taiwan's vTaiwan participatory governance model
to foster greater civic engagement, transparency, and evidence-based policymaking.
Promote Civic Innovation and Social Entrepreneurship:
Establish
Youth Innovation Missions
and civic-tech incubators that support young people in solving public problems through technology, social enterprises, and community-led innovation, aligned with the
Atal Innovation Mission
and
Startup India
.
Adopt a Whole-of-Government Youth Strategy:
Similar to the
European Union Youth Strategy (2019–2027)
, prepare a
National Youth Strategy 2047
with measurable targets on education quality, employment, entrepreneurship, civic participation, mental health, and digital inclusion.
Promote Employment-Intensive Growth:
Complement the
Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme
with incentives for
labour-intensive sectors
such as
textiles, leather, footwear, tourism, and food processing
to generate large-scale employment for youth.
Improve access to affordable credit through initiatives like the
Open Credit Enablement Network (OCEN)
, reduce regulatory burdens, and integrate
MSMEs into Global Value Chains (GVCs)
to expand quality employment opportunities.
Expedite the implementation of the
Code on Social Security, 2020
by establishing
gig-worker welfare boards
, ensuring health insurance, accident coverage, and other social security benefits.

Conclusion

Youth movements should not merely be viewed as episodes of dissent but as
democratic feedback mechanisms.
Harnessing the aspirations, creativity, and civic energy of young people will determine whether India converts its
demographic dividend into a true youth dividend
on the path towards
Viksit Bharat 2047.

Drishti Mains Question:
Q
. Youth aspirations increasingly shape democratic governance in India. Examine the structural factors driving youth disillusionment and suggest policy reforms.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
1. What is the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024?
It is a central law enacted to prevent
paper leaks, cheating, and other unfair practices
in public examinations through stringent penalties and enhanced accountability.
2. What are the key findings of the ILO India Employment Report 2024 on youth employment?
The report states that
youth account for 83% of India's unemployed workforce
, while the unemployment rate among
graduates is 29.1%
, significantly higher than that of non-literate individuals.
3. What is PARAKH under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020?
PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development)
is India's national assessment regulator established to standardise school assessment and improve learning outcomes.
4. What is the 'Youth in All Policies (YiAP)' approach?
Originating in
Finland
, YiAP integrates youth perspectives into policymaking across sectors such as education, employment, health, climate, and technology.

title: Electronic Gold Receipt
content:
Why in News?

India's
Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR)
ecosystem has come into focus as the country's
Gold Exchange
promotes transparent, standardized, and exchange-based trading of physical
gold.

By digitising ownership while retaining the option of physical delivery, EGRs are modernising India's bullion market and strengthening investor confidence.

What is the Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR)?

Gold Exchange Ecosystem:
The
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
-
regulated Gold Exchange creates a national
platform for trading physical gold
in a standardised manner.
It formalises India's fragmented physical gold trade, generating a transparent, real-time domestic spot price for gold.
Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR):
An
EGR
is a
SEBI-regulated electronic security
that represents ownership of
physical gold stored in SEBI-accredited vaults
.
Introduced under India's
Gold Exchange framework
, EGRs enable investors to trade
standardised physical gold
electronically on recognised stock exchanges while retaining the option to convert it into physical gold whenever required.
Unlike physical gold, an EGR is held in
demat form
, making ownership secure, transparent, and easily transferable.
Every EGR is fully backed by an equivalent quantity and purity of physical gold (typically
995 or 999 fineness
) stored with a
SEBI-registered Vault Manager
.
The term
"Receipt"
signifies that every EGR is
100% backed by actual physical gold
, unlike derivative or synthetic products.
An investor holding an EGR becomes the beneficial owner of the corresponding quantity of physical gold without needing to store or transport it.
Need for EGR:
SEBI introduced the Gold Exchange Framework (2022) to address the longstanding challenges of India's
fragmented bullion market, including inconsistent purity standards, opaque pricing, high transaction costs
, and the dominance of unorganised trade.
The framework aims to establish a transparent and regulated national market for physical gold, enable efficient
price discovery, standardise quality, promote investor protection,
and provide a fungible, dematerialised instrument that can be seamlessly converted into physical gold.
Key Participants in the EGR Ecosystem:

Participant
Role
Vault Manager
Stores, verifies, assays, and delivers physical gold under the
SEBI (Vault Managers) Regulations, 2021
.
Depository (NSDL/CDSL)
Maintains EGRs electronically in investors'
demat accounts
.
Stock Exchanges (NSE/BSE)
Provide the trading platform for EGRs.
Stock Brokers
Facilitate buying, selling, and redemption of EGRs.
Investors
Resident individuals, HUFs, NRIs, trusts, institutions, etc., who hold EGRs through demat accounts.

Working of EGR
:
Stage I: Creation:
Eligible
995/999 purity gold
is deposited with a
SEBI-registered Vault Manager
, who verifies and stores it.
The
Depository
then issues equivalent
EGRs
, which are credited to the depositor's
demat account
.
Stage II: Trading:
The issued EGRs are
traded on the NSE and BSE Gold Exchange
, with prices linked to the domestic
spot gold market
.
Ownership changes electronically on a
T+1 settlement basis
, while the physical gold remains securely stored in the vault.
Stage III: Redemption (Withdrawal):
Investors can redeem EGRs for
physical gold
by submitting a request through their
broker or Depository Participant (DP)
.
The
Vault Manager
delivers the gold and simultaneously extinguishes the corresponding EGR from the investor's demat account.
Significance of EGRs:
Unified Price Discovery:
Replaces fragmented and opaque jeweller quotes with a single, transparent
, "One Nation, One Price"
domestic spot price based on real-time supply and demand.
Reduced Import Dependence for Pricing:
A liquid domestic exchange creates an
Indian reference pric
e, making the domestic market less reliant on London (LBMA) or Dubai benchmarks.
Storage and Security:
Removes the burden of locker costs and the risk of theft from individual investors. Vaults are highly secure and fully insured.
Quality Assurance:
Mandatory purity verification at the vaulting stage eliminates the risk of adulteration common in the unorganised physical gold market.
Tax Efficiency:
There is
Zero GST
levied on the trading of EGRs on the exchange. A 3% GST is only applicable if the investor converts the EGR back into physical gold.
Limitations of EGRs:
Despite their advantages, EGRs face challenges such as
limited investor awareness
, relatively low trading volumes, and competition from alternatives like
Gold ETFs, digital gold, and
Sovereign Gold Bonds
(when available)
.
The developing vault infrastructure, additional storage and redemption charges, and GST on physical withdrawal may also constrain wider adoption.

EGR and India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX)
India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX)
,
located in
GIFT City, Gujarat
, is India's
first International Bullion Exchange
, established to facilitate the
import and international trading of bullion
under the
International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA)
.
IIBX supplies standardised bullion
, while
EGRs facilitate its domestic electronic trading
.
Gold imported through
IIBX
can be deposited in
SEBI-accredited vaults
, where it may be converted into
EGRs
after meeting prescribed standards.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
1. What is an Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR)?
An
Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR)
is a
SEBI-regulated electronic security
representing ownership of physical gold stored in SEBI-accredited vaults and held in
demat form
.
2. Why was the Gold Exchange Framework introduced by SEBI?
The framework was introduced to
standardise gold trading, ensure transparent price discovery, improve investor protection, and formalise India's fragmented bullion market
.
3. What is the role of a Vault Manager under the EGR framework?
A
SEBI-registered Vault Manager
verifies, assays, stores, and delivers physical gold while facilitating the issuance and redemption of Electronic Gold Receipts.
4. How is the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) different from the Gold Exchange?
IIBX
, regulated by
IFSCA
, facilitates
international bullion imports and trading
, whereas the
Gold Exchange
, regulated by
SEBI
, enables
domestic trading of Electronic Gold Receipts (EGRs)
.
5. What are the major advantages of Electronic Gold Receipts (EGRs)?
EGRs provide
transparent price discovery, secure electronic ownership, quality assurance, lower storage risks, and seamless conversion into physical gold
, thereby strengthening India's formal bullion market.

UPSC Civil Services Examination, Previous Year Questions (PYQs)
Prelims
:
Q. What is/are the purpose/purposes of Government’s ‘Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme’ and ‘Gold Monetization Scheme’? (2016)
To bring the idle gold lying with Indian households into the economy.
To promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector.
To reduce India’s dependence on gold imports.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Ans:(c)
Q. Which one of the following groups of items is included in India’s foreign-exchange reserves? (2013)
(a) Foreign-currency assets, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) and loans from foreign countries
(b) Foreign-currency assets, gold holdings of the RBI and SDRs
(c) Foreign-currency assets, loans from the World Bank and SDRs
(d) Foreign-currency assets, gold holdings of the RBI and loans from the World Bank
Ans: (b)
Q. Indian Government Bond Yields are influenced by which of the following? (2021)
Actions of the United States Federal Reserve
Actions of the Reserve Bank of India
Inflation and short-term interest rates
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 2 only
(c) 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Ans: (d)

title: India Shines at the 2026 CWG and World Junior Squash Championships Title
content:
The Indian weightlifting and para-powerlifting contingent brought laurels to the nation at the
2026 Commonwealth Games (CWG)
in Glasgow, Scotland
, with
Gyaneshwari Yadav
winning silver and
Jhandu Kumar
securing a historic bronze medal.

In another development, India's
Anahat Singh
created history by becoming the
first Indian to win the girls' singles title
at the
World Junior Squash Championships
.
Gyaneshwari Yadav (Weightlifting):
Won the
silver medal
in the
women's 53 kg
event at the
2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow
.
Nigeria's Onome Omolola Didih
claimed the gold medal with a
206 kg total lift
, setting a
new Commonwealth Games record
.
Jhandu Kumar (Para-Powerlifting):
A para-powerlifter from
Bihar
, secured the
bronze medal
in the
men's heavyweight para-powerlifting
event with a
best lift of 190 kg
, earning
India's first medal
at the
2026 Commonwealth Games
.
He was trained at the
Sports Authority of India (SAI) National Centre of Excellence (NCOE), Gandhinagar
, and is a
Khelo India athlete
, having won
silver at the 2024 Khelo India Para Games
and
gold in 2025
, reflecting the success of the government's sports development initiatives.
Bindyarani Devi Sorokhaibam (Weightlifting):
Won the
bronze medal
in the
women's 58 kg
weightlifting event at the
2026 Commonwealth Games
.
This marked her
second consecutive Commonwealth Games medal
, following her
silver in the 55 kg category at the 2022 Birmingham Games
.

Anahat Singh (Squash)

Achievement:
First Indian to win the World Junior Squash Championships title at the 2026 World Squash Junior Championships in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Canada.
Performance:
Defeated Egypt's Ruqayya Salem in straight games, ending Egypt's 13-title winning streak.
World Junior Squash Championships:
The
official World Junior Squash Championships
were inaugurated in
1980
, while an
unofficial boys' team championship
had been held since
1972
.
The tournament features
squash players under the age of 19
competing in
boys' and girls' individual and team events
.
World Squash
: Established in
1967
, is the
international governing body
for
squash.
It comprises
115 National Squash Federations
.
The
Squash Rackets Federation of India (SRFI)
is the Indian governing body for the game of squash.
World Squash
oversees the
development, governance, and promotion
of the sport globally.
Squash will make its Olympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games.

23rd Commonwealth Games 2026
Mirabai Chanu Wins India's 1st Gold at Commonwealth Games 2026 in Weightlifting
.

title: Teesta Tunnel Disaster: Methane Risks and Himalayan Infrastructure Vulnerability
content:
Why in News?

Recently, a sudden explosive release of suspected
methane and other toxic gases
inside the under-construction H
ead Race Tunnel of the Teesta Stage VI Hydropower Project
at Samardung in
Sikkim’s Namchi district
killed several workers and left others trapped.

The incident highlights the serious safety and geological risks associated with large infrastructure projects in the fragile
Himalayan region.

How Is Methane Trapped in Hilly Terrain?

About Methane:
Methane
is a colourless, odourless and highly flammable gas
that may accumulate naturally in
underground rock formations
and confined spaces such as tunnels.
Explosion Mechanism:
When
methane mixes with air in a particular concentration,
sparks generated by drilling or other construction equipment can ignite it and cause an explosion.
Drilling during the construction of the
Head Race Tunnel
may have disturbed
methane-bearing rocks
, causing the gas to escape suddenly into the tunnel.
Methane in Rocks:
Methane may occur
as natural gas trapped within porous rocks
or as isolated gas pockets in young and fragile geological formations.
Organic Origin:
In mountainous regions with
coal-bearing or carbon-rich strata,
methane can form through the
decomposition of ancient organic matter
over millions of years.
Anaerobic Conditions:
Waterlogged valleys and hilly depressions
may create oxygen-deficient conditions in which
microorganisms
decompose organic material
and release methane.
Migration Through Faults:
Fault lines, cracks and natural fissures
can allow methane from underground coal, gas or geothermal deposits to migrate upward and accumulate in enclosed spaces.
Waste-Related Sources:
Open or
poorly managed waste dumps in hilly areas
can also generate methane when waste decomposes in oxygen-deficient layers.
Sikkim’s Geological Context:
Although Sikkim has no major coalfields, parts of southern Sikkim, including
Namchi, contain small coal deposits
and lie within the geologically complex Rangit Tectonic Window.
Detection Challenge:
Standard geological and engineering surveys assess rock stability,
water conditions and structural risks,
but small and localised methane pockets may remain difficult to identify before excavation.

Why Are Infrastructure Projects in Sikkim Highly Vulnerable?

Teesta-VI Incident:
Although Sikkim’s hydropower projects have previously suffered from
floods and landslides
,
the Teesta-VI tunnel disaster is the
State’s first recorded incident
involving a suspected methane-triggered explosion.
Earlier Project Damage:
The October 2023
Glacial Lake Outburst Flood
destroyed the 1,200 MW Chungthang dam and damaged the 510 MW Teesta-V Hydropower Project, which was affected again by a landslip in August 2024.
Fragile Himalayan Geology:
Sikkim lies in a young,
tectonically active and erosion-prone Himalayan region
, making it highly vulnerable to earthquakes, landslides and slope failures.
Impact of Construction:
Blasting and tunnelling for dams, highways and railways can further disturb unstable slopes and increase the risk of landslides and mudslides.
Human Pressures:
Unregulated
urbanisation
, heavy tourism, deforestation and poor waste management have intensified environmental and geological risks in the State.
Climate-Related Threats:
Cloudbursts
, melting glaciers and expanding glacial lakes have increased the frequency and severity of extreme disasters affecting hydropower infrastructure.

Why Has Tunnelling Been Disaster-Prone in India?

High Geological Risk:
Tunnelling is especially hazardous in the
Himalayan and northeastern regions
because of unstable rocks, active fault lines, heavy rainfall and frequent landslides.
Systemic Failures:
Tunnel disasters often reflect weaknesses in
planning, construction quality, regulatory oversight
and project accountability, rather than geology alone.
Inadequate Risk Assessment:
Incomplete geological surveys, outdated studies and limited predictive modelling may fail to identify
weak rocks, underground water,
fault zones or gas pockets.
Poor Safety Compliance:
Inadequate ventilation, fire protection, escape routes and real-time monitoring can increase the danger faced by underground workers.
Worker Vulnerability:
Limited specialised training,
insufficient protective equipment
and unclear responsibility among contractors and subcontractors further heighten risks.
Need for Reforms:
India requires
stricter safety enforcement,
continuous geological monitoring, clear contractor liability and specialised rescue teams equipped with modern technology.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
1. Where did the Teesta Stage-VI tunnel disaster occur?
The incident occurred inside an under-construction Head Race Tunnel at Samardung in the Namchi district of Sikkim.
2. What was the suspected cause of the explosion?
The explosion is suspected to have resulted from the sudden release and ignition of methane trapped within the surrounding rock formations.
3. How many people died in the incident?
The rescue operation concluded with the recovery of the bodies of all 25 personnel trapped inside the tunnel.
4. What is the capacity of the Teesta Stage-VI Hydroelectric Project?
The run-of-the-river project has an installed capacity of 500 MW, comprising four generating units of 125 MW each.
5. Why is tunnelling difficult in the Himalayas?
The Himalayas consist of young, fractured and tectonically active rocks and are exposed to earthquakes, landslides, intense rainfall, underground water and unexpected geological formations.
